newsitem.title: HAITI: FEATURE - Haiti seeks to resolve age-old bloody land disputes.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Haiti seeks to resolve age-old bloody land disputes.

text.p: Haitian rice farmer Aldolphe Antoine points to the wall of his house and a bullet hole made by an opposing group of farmers who claim rights to the land he once worked in the valley north of Port-au-Prince.

Antoine and fellow farmers working under landowner Sylvio Bricourt have been forced off land they claim is theirs by another landowner, Fouad Attie. Both sides claim they have rights to the land in the Artibonite Valley but neither has the official title.
"Attie is a Lebanese who is not even from here. He has no title to the land, it is our grandparents who were the owners of this land," Antoine said.

Land disputes have sparked such bloody feuds that most Haitian governments did not dare intervene. Settling disputes over land has not been tried seriously since the 1806 assassination of Jean-Jacques Dessalines, Haiti's first emperor, who was killed while attempting such reform.

But current government officials, determined to boost agricultural production in the Western Hemisphere's poorest nation, say solving land disputes is crucial to Haiti's rural development. "It's not just a question of distribution of land, it's a question of rebuilding an entire country," Agriculture Minister Gerald Mathurin said.
AGENCY STEPS IN BETWEEN ARMED, FEUDING CLANS

In April 1995, then-President Jean-Bertrand Aristide signed a decree creating INARA, the National Institute for Agrarian Reform, which has the right to seize land in conflict to be redistributed to peasant farmers. Backed by a specialised SWAT-type unit of the Haitian National Police, INARA is stepping between feuding clans who often are armed with machine guns.

In the dispute between Bricourt and Attie, a decree issued by President Rene Preval gave INARA the right to occupy the land, which they did this month. Peasants were told that after the harvest they were to leave and the land would be redistributed to peasants from both sides of the conflict.

The government's aim is to neutralise the power of intermediaries who manage the farms for landowners. The intermediaries often are former members of the disbanded Haitian army and a paramilitary group, the Revolutionary Front for the Advancement and Progress of Haiti.

"We take the power away from the intermediaries and give it to the peasants who are at their mercy. Very often the intermediaries are more dangerous than the large landowners," said Bernard Etheard, director of INARA.

If the farmers need money to buy seed, fertiliser or tools, they often are forced to borrow it from landowners at interest rates as high as 300 percent, officials said. The landowners live in exclusive enclaves in the capital while farmers cannot afford to send their children to school.

Exacerbating the land problem is Haiti's long history of corruption in the justice system, with judges who can be bought. "Underdeveloped countries have two things in common -- weak justice and no respect for private property," Attie said.

Etheard, appointed by Aristide, took office in July and already is famous in the Artibonite Valley for his tough stand on land conflicts. Four tracts in dispute have been seized by INARA in the last month and Etheard went with police recently to arrest peasants working land after an order was issued for it to be cleared. "It was an example, they will be released," he said.

Because of their inexperience, the Haitian National Police -- formed after Aristide disbanded the army in 1995 -- are restricted to sidearms, hardly a match for the weapons used in the valley. A new police team of up to 150 officers is expected to arrive in the Artibonite and up to ten officers will live in each area where there are land conflicts, according to Pierre Denize, director of the National Police.

"We have proposed an amendment to the current police law so that they would no longer be limited to sidearms," he said. "That doesn't mean the law will change, it just allows specialised units to use adequate weapons for different types of situations."
